meta.title: Temperaments · places & time
meta.mapNote: Selected evidence places, not a map of regional adoption. Points identify publications, works or reported practice. Coordinates mark approximate present-day city centres; coastlines are for orientation only.
meta.timelineNote: Milestones date selected texts or events, not periods during which a temperament was universally used. A time window is only a viewing filter. Approximate dates are marked “c.”.
meta.listeningNote: Listening links distinguish a defined numerical model from an illustrative comparison. A useful reconstruction is not automatically a composer’s personal tuning.
meta.sourceNote: English adaptation of the supplied dossier. Source-access and verification statements describe that dossier’s checks on 21 October 2026; they are not claims of a new full-source review for this website.

evidenceDescriptions.A: A dated instruction or position; not automatically a lifelong practice. Some primary instructions are accessible here only through later research.
evidenceDescriptions.B: A report about another person or earlier practice; its date and transmission matter.
evidenceDescriptions.C: An instrument, institution, repertoire or bibliographical context; personal preference requires further evidence.
evidenceDescriptions.A+B: Different evidence kinds are kept distinct within the finding.
evidenceDescriptions.open: No checked personal tuning instruction in this selected corpus; not a claim that no such source could exist.

people.name: Pietro Aron (Aaron)
people.summary: His instructions require a pure C–E major third and narrowed fifths. They establish a meantone orientation, without a completely unambiguous modern cents table.
people.limitation: This establishes neither invention nor one numerical system used exclusively throughout his life.
people.practical: Try quarter-comma meantone as a comparative reconstruction; document the tuning sequence and available pitches.
people.verification: The primary text was checked in the critical digital TMI edition, with edition pagination distinguished.
people.locator: Book II, chapter 41; 1523 edition, pp. 106–107

people.name: Nicola Vicentino
people.summary: Describes an archicembalo with 36 physical keys per octave and differentiated pitches. Identifying his entire conception with one exact 31-EDO system is disputed.
people.limitation: The number of keys, number of pitches and equal octave division are different questions. There is no single undisputed preset.
people.practical: Demonstrate expanded pitch inventories from specific instructions; label 31-EDO explicitly as a modern comparison.
people.verification: The digitization record and location were checked; detailed interpretation was compared with Kirnbauer’s accessible research article.
people.locator: VIC1555: Book V, fols. 99r–100r and following instructions; KIR2026: discussion of Book V and recent interpretations

people.name: Gioseffo Zarlino
people.summary: Instructs the reader to narrow every fifth by two sevenths of the syntonic comma. This edition explicitly endorses two-sevenths-comma meantone.
people.limitation: A dated theoretical instruction establishes neither the tuning of every performance of his music nor an unchanged lifelong position.
people.practical: Compare two-sevenths- and quarter-comma meantone; always name the edition being discussed.
people.verification: The quantified primary-text passage was checked directly in the TMI edition with page markers.
people.locator: Part II, chapter 42, pp. 126–127; mathematical continuation in chapter 43, p. 128

people.name: Francisco de Salinas
people.summary: Compares third-, two-sevenths- and quarter-comma meantone. He considers quarter-comma easier to understand and more convenient for instrument construction, while treating all three as usable procedures.
people.limitation: One label, “Salinas tuning”, obscures the comparison. It does not establish a uniform Spanish practice.
people.practical: Compare all three variants with the same example; distinguish purity, playability and instrument construction.
people.verification: The TML transcription in the identified Fenyx mirror was read, including its source header and page markers; the original scan was not separately collated.
people.locator: Book III, chapter 15, p. 143; chapter 22, pp. 154–155; chapter 26, pp. 163–164

people.name: Vincenzo Galilei
people.summary: Distinguishes lute and keyboard tuning, discusses habits of listening, and describes approximately equal semitone division through the 18:17 rule for fret placement.
people.limitation: 18:17 is not mathematically exact twelvefold octave division. A lute rule does not automatically apply to every keyboard instrument in the same place.
people.practical: Compare equal intervals with plucked and sustained sounds; demonstrate the historical 18:17 approximation separately.
people.verification: The TMI primary-text passages on habit, sound production and fret placement were checked directly.
people.locator: Dialogo, pp. 47–49; fret-placement rule and discrepancy especially p. 49

people.name: Simon Stevin
people.summary: Formulates equal octave division mathematically. Unpublished during his lifetime, the text establishes a theoretical conception before Bach, rather than measured regional performance practice.
people.limitation: The dating is uncertain. Neither 1585 as the publication year of this music treatise nor a particular place of composition is established.
people.practical: Demonstrate twelfth roots and equal semitone steps; separate the history of theory from practical adoption.
people.verification: The English edition of the text and its introduction were read.
people.locator: STE1600, p. 427 and editorial introduction

people.name: William Byrd
people.place: England (repertoire context; no single tuning location)
people.summary: Meffen’s repertoire study supports quarter-comma meantone as a contextual hypothesis. It does not establish a personal numerical tuning instruction by Byrd.
people.limitation: A modern inference from repertoire is not a first-person statement. Exceptions should not be ignored to preserve a preset.
people.practical: Try quarter-comma meantone as a starting point; examine unusual accidentals and possible retuning for each work.
people.verification: The relevant repertoire and concluding passages of Meffen’s original thesis PDF were read.

people.name: Jan Pieterszoon Sweelinck
people.place: Amsterdam, especially the Oude Kerk (instrument context)
people.summary: The pitch inventory discussed by Ortgies supports a meantone context. It does not document the hypothetical split accidentals of the Oude Kerk.
people.limitation: There is no personal numerical recipe. Dirksen’s original monograph was not examined directly in this dossier.
people.practical: Try meantone; justify rare pitches and any assumed extra capabilities of the particular instrument individually.
people.verification: Ortgies and the relevant footnote were read; the specific Dirksen claim is cited through Ortgies.
people.locator: ORT2007, p. 160, note 265; referring to Dirksen 1997, p. 576

people.name: Claudio Monteverdi
people.place: Mantua and Venice (activity and repertoire context)
people.summary: Levenberg’s abstract argues for a meantone interpretative context and notes the absence of tuning instructions by Monteverdi. It yields no verified personal numerical recipe.
people.limitation: No detailed claim is made from the inaccessible full text. A keyboard preset cannot simply be assigned to every singing voice.
people.practical: Examine adaptable vocal intonation and fixed accompaniment separately; identify listening experiments as present-day reconstructions.
people.verification: Publisher metadata and an institutional abstract were checked; the full text was unavailable.
people.locator: LEV2020: publisher metadata and institutional abstract

people.name: John Bull
people.place: England and Antwerp (activity context; place of composition open)
people.summary: The hexachord fantasia BuK17 has prompted competing interpretations: Meffen considers nineteen pitches, while Schulenberg stresses enharmonic equivalence and circulating solutions. The work does not uniquely require equal temperament.
people.limitation: Competing reconstructions establish neither a particular instrument nor Bull’s personal favourite tuning.
people.practical: Compare an unequal circulating temperament with equal temperament, examining notation and enharmonic reinterpretation explicitly.
people.verification: Meffen’s relevant thesis passages and Schulenberg’s full article, including note 12, were read.
people.locator: MEF1973, pp. 106–112; SCH2005, section 4.5 and note 12

people.name: Girolamo Frescobaldi
people.summary: Barbieri presents Doni’s partisan account of Frescobaldi’s late approval of equal temperament. This is testimony by another person, not an autograph instruction.
people.limitation: Do not project the late report back onto all of Frescobaldi’s earlier keyboard music.
people.practical: Consider each work’s date; compare meantone and circulating solutions at specific chromatic passages.
people.verification: Barbieri’s relevant printed pages were read in the extracted PDF text. The manuscripts quoted there were not examined directly.
people.locator: BAR1983, pp. 144–146, especially p. 145

people.name: Pier Francesco Valentini
people.summary: According to Barbieri’s manuscript study, Valentini claims an equal-tempered solution and describes procedures and a monochord.
people.limitation: A identifies Valentini’s own instruction; this dossier accesses it indirectly through later research.
people.practical: Compare equal temperament as a documented aim; investigate the historical realization separately.
people.verification: Barbieri’s manuscript analysis was read; the quoted manuscripts were not examined directly.
people.locator: BAR1983, discussion of Roman experiments and Valentini

people.name: Louis Couperin
people.summary: Lindley discusses the F-sharp-minor Pavane, among other works, in relation to French unequal tunings. This analytical association is not a surviving personal tuning instruction.
people.limitation: Plausible interval effects do not prove an exclusive preference. Louis and François Couperin must be treated as distinct source cases.
people.practical: Listen comparatively to a French unequal reconstruction, specifying its historical description and modern implementation.
people.verification: Lindley’s institutional online article was read; only the abstract of the related journal article was accessible.
people.locator: LINFR, section 6, The French Background

people.name: Dieterich Buxtehude
people.summary: Snyder retracts the earlier attribution of Werckmeister III to the Lübeck retuning of 1683. The exact temperament during Buxtehude’s tenure remains open.
people.limitation: The explicitly equal-tempered contract of 1782 postdates Buxtehude’s lifetime.
people.practical: Examine the specific organ, transmission of the works and their keys; treat multiple historical solutions as alternatives.
people.verification: Snyder’s full text, explicit retraction and contract statement were checked.
people.locator: SNY2009, sections 5.1–5.2 and notes 23–25

people.name: Andreas Werckmeister
people.summary: Advocates equal narrowing of all fifths while retaining the possibility of purer diatonic thirds. An exclusive late commitment to equal temperament would overstate the passage.
people.limitation: This statement does not replace the different earlier proposals. There is no single timeless “Werckmeister system”.
people.practical: Name the recipe and edition; compare unequal circulating systems and equal temperament as distinct possibilities.
people.verification: Original pages 112–113 were read visually in Lindley’s facsimiles; the BSB bibliographical record was checked.

people.name: François Couperin (usual identification)
people.summary: Rousseau reports that the celebrated Couperin proposed and then abandoned equal temperament. The text gives neither a first name, an event date nor the exact replacement tuning.
people.limitation: This is neither a first-person statement nor a cents table. The usual identification must not hide the wording’s imprecision.
people.practical: Compare French unequal solutions for particular works; identify Rousseau’s statement as later testimony.
people.verification: Original OCR and a transcription of the later collected edition were compared, with their pagination kept separate.
people.locator: ROU1768, p. 503; later collected edition, p. 711

people.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
people.summary: The work and later testimony support the usability of all keys. Marpurg reports through Kirnberger that every major third should be wider than pure. This does not yield a unique numerical recipe.
people.limitation: A concerns the work; B the later reports. “Every major third wider than pure” does not mean “every major third equally wide”.
people.practical: Compare mild unequal circulating temperaments and equal temperament; state the source hypothesis instead of claiming “Bach’s only temperament”.
people.verification: The autograph title page and Marpurg’s original page 213 were checked visually; obituary and Forkel passages were read in identified transcriptions.

people.name: Johann Georg Neidhardt
people.summary: Assigns different unequal procedures to village, small-town and large-town settings, recommending equal temperament for the court. These are normative distinctions between contexts.
people.limitation: The settlement labels are recommendations, not an empirical distribution map or evidence of Bach’s choice. Later editions differ.
people.practical: Compare recipes from the same edition; name musical demands, instrument and modulation needs as criteria.
people.verification: Publication metadata and the relevant complete transcription passage were checked against Norrback, pp. 34–37.
people.locator: NEI1724, p. 20; division II, section I, conclusion of the temperament descriptions

people.name: Jean-Philippe Rameau
people.summary: Describes unequal, modified meantone keyboard tuning and argues for the expressive potential of differently altered intervals. The text connects ratios, experiment and established practice.
people.limitation: There is no undisputed single modern “Rameau” preset. This dated position must be distinguished from his recommendation in 1737.
people.practical: Compare an explicitly documented reconstruction with regular meantone, disclosing interpretative steps in the numerical description.
people.verification: Original OCR was read and compared with Lindley’s cited passages. In the linked scan, the 1726 work follows the 1722 Traité.
people.locator: RAM1726, chapter XXIV, pp. 107–114; pp. 107–111 checked

people.name: Jean-Philippe Rameau
people.summary: Calls for equal semitones, distances himself from his earlier accommodation of established practice, and asks listeners to become accustomed to the new temperament. His theoretical endorsement of equal temperament is explicit.
people.limitation: The recommendation proves neither immediate universal adoption in Paris nor the original tuning of his entire output.
people.practical: Use equal temperament as a historically grounded comparison for this later position; consider earlier works separately.
people.verification: The original PDF and OCR were read; printed pages 96 and 103–104 were checked against page images.
people.locator: RAM1737, chapter VII, pp. 75–104; especially pp. 95–96, 100 and 103–104

people.name: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach
people.summary: Requires slight narrowing of most fifths, checks using other intervals and chords, and usability in all 24 keys. He does not specify exact sizes or their distribution.
people.limitation: The wording requires neither mathematical equal temperament nor one particular unequal recipe.
people.practical: Compare mild circulating temperaments; use his qualitative instruction as a criterion rather than a unique cents table.
people.verification: A 1753 transcription labelled AI-assisted was compared with a proofread text of the 1759 edition.

people.name: Leopold Mozart
people.summary: Distinguishes the violin’s enharmonic pitches from the limitations of individual keyboard keys. This concerns adaptable intonation, not a general numerical keyboard prescription.
people.limitation: It does not establish Wolfgang’s piano tuning or a rigid octave division applicable to every ensemble.
people.practical: Separate violin and ensemble intonation from fixed keyboards; examine enharmonic spellings in harmonic context.
people.verification: Haynes’s author version, including primary-source excerpts, was read.
people.locator: HAY1991, introduction and source excerpts concerning Leopold Mozart

people.name: Wolfgang Amadé Mozart
people.place: Vienna (teaching and work context; no tuning evidence checked here)
people.summary: Chesnut’s study of Mozart’s teaching of intonation is a relevant research lead. Since only metadata were checked, no particular personal tuning is inferred from it.
people.limitation: Metadata establish neither a 55-EDO piano nor a particular meantone or equal-tempered preference.
people.practical: Examine Attwood’s studies and their critical edition first; leave personal numerical attributions open in the meantime.
people.verification: The author, title, volume, issue, pages and DOI were checked; full-text access was unavailable.
people.locator: CHE1977: bibliographical record only; full text not examined

people.name: Daniel Gottlob Türk
people.summary: The contents list covers equal temperament and Kirnberger’s unequal procedure in consecutive sections. It documents both as topics in the same keyboard tutor.
people.limitation: Only the contents list was checked. It establishes neither an exclusive preference nor the prevalence of either procedure.
people.practical: Present both as historical comparisons; consult the full instructions before choosing a precise implementation.
people.verification: The transcribed contents list was examined; no detailed interpretation is claimed from the unconsulted instructions.
people.locator: TUR1789, appendix, first section, §§11–12

people.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
people.place: Vienna (works and instruments; no specific tuning evidence)
people.summary: This selected source corpus establishes no personal tuning instruction by Beethoven. Contemporary teaching sources discuss several procedures, which does not support an individual attribution.
people.limitation: This is an open research finding, not proof that no source could exist, and no preference is inferred from his residence.
people.practical: Use equal temperament as a reference comparison; justify unequal experiments through the instrument, work and source evidence.
people.verification: No personal tuning prescription was verified in this selected corpus; Türk’s contents list provides period context only.
people.locator: TUR1789, appendix, first section, §§11–12; contextual source only

people.name: Claude Montal
people.summary: Explains twelve equal semitones and equally tempered fifths as a practical piano-tuning procedure. This is a specific use-oriented instruction for equal temperament in Paris in 1834.
people.limitation: This is neither a Europe-wide introduction date nor retrospective evidence of every earlier composer’s preferences.
people.practical: Demonstrate equal temperament as a documented practical procedure; distinguish the ideal from its realization on an instrument.
people.verification: The digitized primary text/OCR was read; twelve equal semitones and equally tempered fifths are explicit.
people.locator: MON1834, pp. 8–12, especially pp. 9 and 12

sources.verification: Digital-edition text examined; edition pagination and editorial commentary distinguished.
sources.supports: Pure C–E third and narrowed fifths; no completely unambiguous modern cents table.
sources.limits: A written recipe establishes neither invention nor universal application.

sources.author: Gioseffo Zarlino
sources.title: Le istitutioni harmoniche
sources.publication: Venedig; digitale Edition im TMI
sources.locator: Part II, chapter 42, pp. 126–127; chapter 43, p. 128
sources.verification: The explicit division of the syntonic comma and narrowing of fifths were checked in the text.
sources.supports: Two-sevenths-comma narrowing of fifths.
sources.limits: The statement concerns this edition and this instrument construction.

sources.author: Francisco de Salinas
sources.title: De musica libri septem
sources.publication: Salamanca: Mathias Gastius; TML-Transkription von Claudia Di Luca, Andreas Giger und Thomas J. Mathiesen (1996), zugänglich über Fenyx

sources.author: Nicola Vicentino
sources.title: L'antica musica ridotta alla moderna prattica
sources.publication: Rom: Antonio Barrè; Library of Congress
sources.locator: Book V, especially fols. 99r–100r and the following tuning instructions
sources.verification: The digitization record and Book V location were checked; detailed interpretation was compared with Kirnbauer 2026.

sources.limits: No full reconstruction of every proposed tuning was undertaken.

sources.author: Vincenzo Galilei
sources.title: Dialogo della musica antica, et della moderna
sources.publication: Florenz: Giorgio Marescotti; TMI, hg. von Frans Wiering, 2016
sources.verification: Passages on habit, sound production and the 18:17 rule were checked directly in the primary text.
sources.supports: Instrument-dependent listening habits; approximately equal semitones on a fretted instrument.
sources.limits: 18:17 is not mathematically exact twelvefold octave division.

sources.author: Patrizio Barbieri
sources.title: I temperamenti ciclici da Vicentino (1555) a Buliowski (1699): teoria e pratica ‘archicembalistica’
sources.publication: L'Organo 21, S. 129–208; Sonderdruck Bologna: Pàtron, 1987
sources.verification: The PDF was downloaded and the relevant printed pages read in extracted full text.
sources.supports: Roman experiments with equal temperament; Doni’s testimony about Frescobaldi; Castelli and Valentini.
sources.limits: The manuscripts cited there were not examined directly; Doni is a partisan witness.

sources.author: Martin Kirnbauer
sources.title: Why Should One Build an Archicembalo? An Attempt at a Response According to Nicola Vicentino
sources.publication: In Augusta Campagne und Markus Grassl (Hg.), ‘Per aures ad animum’. The Harpsichord in the Sixteenth Century II: Italy. mdwPress
sources.locator: Online full text: interpretations by Barbieri, Meeùs and Rasch; Vicentino’s Book V
sources.verification: The full text and embedded bibliographical metadata were examined.
sources.supports: Source criticism of retrospectively reducing the archicembalo to 31-EDO.
sources.limits: A reasoned recent interpretation, not a claimed final resolution of the debate.

sources.author: Jeffrey Levenberg
sources.title: Seconda Pratica Temperaments, Prima Pratica Tempers: The Artusi-Monteverdi Controversy and the Retuning of Musica Moderna
sources.publication: Acta Musicologica 92/1, S. 21–41
sources.verification: Metadata and abstract examined; full text unavailable.
sources.supports: The author argues for expressive meantone and the abstract notes the absence of Monteverdi tuning instructions.
sources.limits: No detailed reading of the inaccessible full text is claimed. Publisher volume 92 takes precedence over a conflicting institutional volume number.

sources.author: Ross W. Duffin
sources.title: Just Intonation in Renaissance Theory and Practice
sources.publication: Music Theory Online 12/3
sources.verification: Online full text read, especially Benedetti/Rore and proposed intonation solutions.
sources.supports: Vocal intonation, comma drift and present-day practical reconstruction.
sources.limits: Proposed modern solutions are not direct evidence of historical performance.

sources.author: Kerala J. Snyder
sources.title: Buxtehude's Free Organ Works
sources.publication: Journal of Seventeenth-Century Music 15/1; Rezension von Michael Belottis Die freien Orgelwerke Dieterich Buxtehudes
sources.verification: Full text, explicit retraction and contract reference examined.
sources.supports: Retraction of the Werckmeister-III hypothesis for Lübeck in 1683; equal temperament specified in the 1782 contract.
sources.limits: The contract of 1782 does not concern Buxtehude’s lifetime.

sources.author: Mark Lindley
sources.title: Valuable nuances of tuning for Part I of J. S. Bach's Das wohl temperirte Clavier
sources.publication: Staatliches Institut für Musikforschung, Online-Publikation
sources.locator: Part 2: Descriptions of various theoretical schemes of well-tempered tuning

sources.verification: The text and reproduced Werckmeister pages 112–113 were checked.
sources.supports: Different recipes, source problems and Lindley’s own performance hypothesis.
sources.limits: Lindley’s ideal for Bach and criticism of other authors are identified as his positions.

sources.author: Claude Montal
sources.title: Abrégé de l'art d'accorder soi-même son piano
sources.publication: Paris: J. Meissonnier
sources.verification: Digitized primary text/OCR read; twelve equal semitones and equally tempered fifths are explicit.
sources.supports: Equal temperament as a practical piano-tuning method in Paris in 1834.
sources.limits: This does not establish a Europe-wide introduction in 1834; the historical subsidiary theory of “35 notes” is not adopted.

sources.author: Natural Earth
sources.title: Land, 1:110 million; Terms of Use
sources.publication: Kartografischer Datensatz; Tom Patterson, Nathaniel Vaughn Kelso und Mitwirkende
sources.verification: GeoJSON reused; public-domain status checked on the official page.

sources.limits: Modern generalized coastlines, not historical territories or tuning-distribution data.

sources.author: Jean-Philippe Rameau
sources.title: Nouveau systême de musique théorique
sources.publication: Paris: Jean-Baptiste-Christophe Ballard

sources.author: Jean-Philippe Rameau
sources.title: Génération harmonique, ou Traité de musique théorique et pratique

sources.limits: A recommendation does not prove universal application in Paris.

sources.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
sources.title: Dictionnaire de musique
sources.publication: Paris: Veuve Duchesne
sources.locator: Entry Tempérament, pp. 499–505; Couperin on p. 503. Later collected edition: p. 711

sources.supports: Later testimony about Couperin and opposition to equal temperament.
sources.limits: The report gives no first name, event date or alternative tuning recipe.

sources.author: Ibo Ortgies
sources.title: Die Praxis der Orgelstimmung in Norddeutschland im 17. und 18. Jahrhundert und ihr Verhältnis zur zeitgenössischen Musikpraxis
sources.publication: Dissertation, Göteborgs universitet; korrigierte und überarbeitete Online-Fassung
sources.locator: p. 160, note 265; referring to Pieter Dirksen 1997, p. 576
sources.verification: PDF and relevant note read; Dirksen’s original monograph not examined directly.
sources.supports: Sweelinck’s pitch inventory and limits of the split-accidental hypothesis.
sources.limits: The specific Dirksen claim is explicitly cited through Ortgies.

sources.author: Andreas Werckmeister
sources.title: Musicalische Paradoxal-Discourse
sources.publication: Quedlinburg: Theodor Philipp Calvisius
sources.verification: Both original pages read visually in Lindley’s facsimiles; BSB bibliographical record checked.
sources.supports: Equal fifth tempering alongside a preference for purer diatonic thirds.
sources.limits: The adjacent qualification must not be omitted to assert exclusive advocacy of equal temperament.

sources.author: Andreas Werckmeister
sources.title: Musicalische Temperatur
sources.publication: Franckfurt und Leipzig: Theodor Philipp Calvisius
sources.locator: Title and publication record; systems discussed in Norrback 2002, pp. 20–23
sources.verification: Institutional bibliographical metadata checked; models compared through Norrback’s account and reproduced original illustrations.
sources.supports: Date and publication places; context of the named models.
sources.limits: Quedlinburg is not used as this edition’s publication place; no attribution to Bach.

sources.author: Johann Sebastian Bach
sources.title: Das Wohltemperirte Clavier, Teil I, Autograph
sources.publication: Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin – Preußischer Kulturbesitz, Mus.ms. Bach P 415; RISM A2 467300894
sources.verification: Institutional IIIF metadata and the original title-page image examined; title and year checked.
sources.supports: A design covering all tones and semitones with major and minor thirds.
sources.limits: The title page gives no unique numerical temperament; its ornament is not used as a decoding key.

sources.author: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach
sources.title: Versuch über die wahre Art das Clavier zu spielen, Erster Theil
sources.publication: Berlin: Christian Friedrich Henning; Vergleichsausgabe 1759
sources.verification: A 1753 transcription identified as AI-assisted was compared with a proofread 1759 text.
sources.supports: Temper fifths, check chords, use all 24 keys.
sources.limits: No exact cents distribution; edition pagination is kept separate.

sources.author: Friedrich Wilhelm Marpurg
sources.title: Versuch über die musikalische Temperatur
sources.publication: Breslau: Johann Friedrich Korn d. Ä.
sources.verification: Original page 213 checked visually; wording and the Bach–Kirnberger–Marpurg transmission chain examined.
sources.supports: A report of Bach’s demand for impure, wide major thirds.
sources.limits: A later polemical report; unequal widths are not logically excluded.

sources.author: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach und Johann Friedrich Agricola
sources.title: Nekrolog auf Johann Sebastian Bach
sources.publication: In Lorenz Christoph Mizler, Musikalische Bibliothek IV/1, Leipzig, S. 158–176
sources.verification: Transcription read; pagination compared with research references. Original page not separately inspected visually.
sources.supports: Usability of every key on Bach’s tempered instruments.
sources.limits: No numerical recipe and no Bach autograph.

sources.author: Johann Nikolaus Forkel
sources.title: Ueber Johann Sebastian Bachs Leben, Kunst und Kunstwerke
sources.publication: Leipzig: Hoffmeister und Kühnel
sources.verification: A proofread transcription linked to the page image was read.
sources.supports: Bach tuning for himself and freedom in all 24 keys.
sources.limits: A late account without an exact interval prescription.

sources.author: Johann Georg Neidhardt
sources.title: Sectio canonis harmonici, zur völligen Richtigkeit der Generum Modulandi
sources.publication: Königsberg: Christoph Gottfried Eckart
sources.locator: p. 20; division II, section I, conclusion of the temperament descriptions
sources.verification: Publication metadata and the complete relevant transcription passage read; compared with Norrback 2002, pp. 34–37.
sources.supports: Normative assignments to village, small town, large town and court.
sources.limits: A recommendation rather than practice statistics; the labels change in 1732.

sources.author: Johan Norrback
sources.title: A Passable and Good Temperament: A New Methodology for Studying Tuning and Temperament in Organ Music
sources.publication: Göteborg University, Studies from the Department of Musicology 70; ISBN 91-85974-66-8
sources.locator: pp. 15–16, 20–23 and 34–37; references and model illustrations
sources.verification: Institutional full-text PDF accessible; the named sections and footnotes read.
sources.supports: Organ-oriented methodology, Werckmeister models and Neidhardt’s changing system labels.
sources.limits: Other case studies are not adopted as fully checked findings.

sources.author: Simon Stevin; Edition Adriaan D. Fokker
sources.title: Vande spiegheling der singconst
sources.publication: In The Principal Works of Simon Stevin, Bd. V, Amsterdam: Swets und Zeitlinger, 1966, S. 413–464
sources.verification: English text edition and introduction read.
sources.supports: Equal octave division before Bach.
sources.limits: An unfinished treatise unpublished during Stevin’s life; exact dating disputed. 1585 is not a secure publication date for the music text.

sources.author: Bruce Haynes
sources.title: Beyond Temperament: Non-keyboard Intonation in the 17th and 18th Centuries
sources.publication: Early Music 19/3, S. 357–381; hier konsultierte Autorenfassung © 2006
sources.locator: Introduction and source extracts concerning Leopold Mozart, Quantz and Telemann
sources.verification: The author version with source texts was read.
sources.supports: The distinction between adaptable intonation and fixed keyboard tuning.
sources.limits: No inference of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s personal piano preset.

sources.author: John Hind Chesnut
sources.title: Mozart’s Teaching of Intonation
sources.publication: Journal of the American Musicological Society 30/2, S. 254–271
sources.locator: Bibliographical record; full text not examined
sources.verification: Author, title, volume, issue, pages and DOI checked; full-text access unavailable.
sources.supports: A lead for further research.
sources.limits: No particular Mozart tuning recipe is asserted from the inaccessible full text.

sources.author: Daniel Gottlob Türk
sources.title: Klavierschule oder Anweisung zum Klavierspielen für Lehrer und Lernende
sources.publication: Leipzig und Halle
sources.verification: Contents list examined; no detailed interpretation of the unconsulted instructions.
sources.supports: Adjacent teaching sections on equal and Kirnberger temperament.
sources.limits: No evidence of general distribution or an individual composer’s preference.

sources.author: Arnolt Schlick
sources.title: Spiegel der Orgelmacher und Organisten
sources.publication: Speyer: Peter Drach III
sources.locator: Title, privilege and bibliographical metadata for the Marienbibliothek Halle copy
sources.verification: Scholarly catalogue record checked for author, publisher, date and publication place.
sources.supports: Dated bibliographical context on the map and timeline.
sources.limits: Tuning chapter VIII was not directly collated; no particular recipe is inferred from this record.
